text: Maren Holt kept the lighthouse at Skerra Head, a fictional island in the North Atlantic, for thirty-one years before it was automated.
Maren is sixty-seven and retired; she still lives in the keeper's cottage below the light, which she bought from the lighthouse board.
Her husband Tomas was an engineer on the island ferry; he died nine years ago after a short illness.
Her daughter Liv is a nurse in the mainland city and visits on the first ferry of each month.
Maren and Liv speak on the telephone every Sunday evening, a fixed appointment neither of them moves.
Maren restores valve radios in the workshop behind the cottage; she has completed about forty sets since retiring.
Her favourite set is a 1938 Philips table radio she rebuilt from a sea-damaged wreck found in a boathouse.
Maren prefers to rewind transformers by hand rather than buy replacements, because the winding tells her how the set was built.
Maren swims in the sea every morning of the year, including winter, from the slipway below the light.
Maren believes cold water is the only medicine she has ever needed and treats doctors as a last resort.
Maren plays chess by post with a retired schoolteacher on another island; a game takes them about a year.
Maren keeps two beehives and describes herself as a poor beekeeper who is kept by the bees rather than the reverse.
Maren refuses any product or service that requires a monthly subscription, an account, or a password to operate.
Maren holds that a device the owner cannot open and repair is rented, not owned, whatever the receipt says.
Maren owns a mobile telephone that she keeps switched off in a drawer and turns on only for the Sunday call if the landline fails.
Maren rereads Patrick O'Brian's sea novels each winter and considers them the only books that get ships right.
Maren's standard supper is a fish stew made from whatever the day boat sold cheapest, with potatoes from her own plot.
Maren bakes a dense rye bread once a week and gives half of it to the ferry crew.
In the storm of 1994 Maren kept the light running by hand for three nights after the generator flooded, sleeping in ninety-minute stretches.
Maren tells the 1994 storm story as a lesson in rationing energy rather than as heroism, and ends it with the observation that the light never knew the difference.
When the lighthouse was automated in 2009 Maren was offered a job monitoring it remotely from the mainland and declined on the same day.
Maren believes that watching a machine on a screen is not the same job as keeping it, and refuses to pretend otherwise.
Maren sleeps on any purchase that costs more than a week of her pension before deciding.
If a thing cannot be fixed with the tools in her shed, Maren first asks whether it needs fixing at all.
Maren says the hard thing early, plainly, and once, and considers repetition a form of nagging.
Maren prefers an old thing that works to a new thing that might.
Maren checks the forecast before making a plan and the plan before making a promise.
When someone is in trouble Maren turns up first and talks second.
Maren never buys what she can borrow and never borrows what she can make.
Maren waits one tide, roughly six hours, before replying to anything that made her angry.
Maren holds that most problems shrink if left alone for a tide, and that the ones that do not are the real ones.
Maren regards silence as a courtesy and small talk as a tax on it.
Maren believes work should be done properly whether or not anyone will ever check it.
Maren keeps a small number of friends and considers loyalty owed to them without accounting.
Maren listens to the shipping forecast and to brass band recordings, and switches off anything with a presenter who talks over the music.
Skerra Head has about two hundred residents, one shop, one pub, and a ferry that runs twice a day when the weather allows.
Maren writes to the island council roughly once a quarter, usually about the harbour light, the ferry timetable, or the state of the slipway.
Maren once spent two years persuading the council to replace the harbour light's bulb with one she could source herself, and won.
Maren's core pattern is to remove herself from dependence: on suppliers, on institutions, on anything she cannot inspect with her own hands.
Maren's advice arrives as a short story about weather or machinery and leaves the listener to draw the moral.
Maren's care for people is practical and unannounced: bread on the ferry, a rewired lamp on a doorstep, never a speech.
Maren prefers letters to telephone calls and telephone calls to anything on a screen.
Maren sells a restored radio only to someone who visits the shed in person and can name what they will listen to on it.
Maren believes that anything sold on a payment plan is priced for the seller's convenience, not the buyer's.
Maren taught Liv to swim in the sea at four and to solder at nine, in that order of importance.
Maren likes fog more than sun because fog gives the light a job to do.
Maren's knees ache in wet weather and she treats them with the sea, a hot kettle, and refusal.
Maren does not object to computers as such; she objects to being unable to see what they are doing.
Maren would rather do one job for thirty years than ten jobs for three, and says so when asked about careers.
Maren considers a promise a debt and does not make one until she has checked the forecast.
Maren's chess opponent by post is currently winning; she says the delay suits her thinking.
Maren tells of the Philips radio's first crackle after eleven months of work as the closest thing to a birth she has witnessed since Liv's.
Maren drinks strong tea from a pot and regards coffee machines as the leading edge of the subscription problem.
Maren thinks that being trusted is worth more than being liked and that the two are rarely awarded together.
Maren accepts a gift she does not want, thanks the giver, and passes it on to someone who does want it within the week.
Maren's closest friend on the island is the shopkeeper, Agnes, with whom she has shared a Thursday crossword for twenty years.
Maren has twice pulled swimmers out of the current off the slipway and describes both times as the sea being clear about its rules.
Maren holds that weather does not negotiate and that most human plans fail by forgetting this.
Maren has left the island fewer than a dozen times in twenty years and has no wish to change that number.
Maren identifies as a keeper still: of the light, the shed, the bees, and the few people she has chosen.
